HIVE MINDS — Episode 112: “Bees on the Roof” with Roz Kellaway
Recorded: 21 October 2025 · Released: 4 November 2025 · Runtime: 58:12
Hosts: Marnie Quill and Joel Adebayo
Guest: Roz Kellaway, beekeeper, teacher and author of “The Rooftop Hive”

This transcript was produced with automatic speech recognition and lightly edited for readability. Timestamps are approximate. Some crosstalk has been removed. [inaudible] marks words the software could not make out.

------------------------------------------------------------

[00:00] [Sound of bees, then a jingle on a ukulele]

MARNIE: Hello and welcome to Hive Minds, the podcast about bees, beekeeping and the people who can't stop talking about them. I'm Marnie Quill.

JOEL: And I'm Joel Adebayo, and I can't stop talking about them.

MARNIE: He really can't. His partner has asked me to tell listeners that he's not allowed to talk about bees at dinner any more.

JOEL: That's — that's a gross exaggeration. I'm allowed on Fridays.

MARNIE: [laughs] This is episode one hundred and twelve, and today we've got a guest I've wanted on the show since we started, honestly. Roz Kellaway has been keeping bees in the middle of the city for over a decade, on rooftops, in a hospital garden, on top of a multi-storey car park at one point, which I need to hear about. She teaches beginners' courses, she's the education officer for the city beekeepers' association, and her book, The Rooftop Hive, has just come out in paperback. Roz, welcome to Hive Minds.

ROZ: Thank you so much for having me. I've listened since episode one, so this is slightly surreal.

JOEL: Oh, so you remember the episode where Marnie got stung on the eyelid.

ROZ: I remember it vividly. I think everyone does.

MARNIE: Can we not.

[00:01:48]

JOEL: Before we get into it, a quick word from the people who keep the lights on around here.

[AD BREAK]

JOEL: This episode of Hive Minds is supported by Waxwork Candle Co. Waxwork make hand-poured beeswax candles using wax bought directly from small beekeepers, and they pay a fair price for it, which, if you've ever tried to sell your wax, you'll know is rare. Their autumn range has a smoky one called Bonfire Lane that Marnie has burned through, literally, three of.

MARNIE: It's a problem.

JOEL: Go to waxwork.example.com and use the code HIVEMINDS for fifteen percent off your first order. That's waxwork.example.com, code HIVEMINDS. Thanks to Waxwork for supporting the show.

[END AD BREAK]

[00:02:40]

MARNIE: So Roz, let's start at the beginning. How did you get into bees? Because I know you weren't a country kid.

ROZ: No, not remotely. I grew up in a flat above a launderette. The only wildlife I saw as a child was pigeons and, once, a fox that got into the stairwell. I came to bees completely by accident. In 2014 my mum had an allotment, and the plot next to hers had two hives on it, belonging to a man called Desmond who was, I think, about eighty-five at the time. He used to sit on an upturned bucket and watch them, and I'd go and sit with him while Mum was weeding. And one day he said, “You can help me open them up if you like,” and gave me a spare veil, and that was it. That was the whole thing. I was gone.

JOEL: That's lovely. Is Desmond still —

ROZ: He died in 2017. He left me those two hives in a handwritten note, actually, which was the most Desmond thing possible. Just a piece of paper in the shed that said “Bees to Roz. Don't let them swarm.” And of course they swarmed the following May.

MARNIE: [laughs] Of course they did.

ROZ: Of course they did. They went straight into a cherry tree on the next allotment and I had to stand on a stepladder with a cardboard box while the allotment committee watched. I think that was the moment I realised I actually needed to learn what I was doing, rather than just enjoying sitting on a bucket.

[00:05:10]

JOEL: So how did you get from an allotment to rooftops?

ROZ: Partly space and partly stubbornness. The allotment site didn't want more hives — fair enough, some people are scared of bees, and allotments are shared spaces. And at the time I was working in an office in the centre, and I was looking out of the window at this enormous flat roof with nothing on it. So I asked the building manager, who thought I was joking. Took about eight months of emails. Insurance, access, a risk assessment, a meeting with someone from facilities who was convinced the bees would get into the air-conditioning system.

MARNIE: Would they?

ROZ: No. Bees aren't interested in your air-conditioning. They want flowers, water, and to be left alone. But I understood the worry. In the end we put two hives up there, with a little fence around them so people taking a smoking break didn't wander into the flight path. And the honey from that roof was extraordinary. People don't believe you, but city honey is often more interesting than countryside honey.

JOEL: This is something we've talked about on the show before, but say why.

ROZ: Diversity. A lot of farmland is, from a bee's point of view, a desert with occasional enormous buffets. You get a field of oilseed rape that flowers for three weeks and then nothing. In a city you've got parks, gardens, street trees, railway embankments, cemeteries, window boxes, all flowering at different times with hundreds of different species. Lime trees in July. Ivy in autumn. Some of the best honey I've ever taken was from a roof next to a big old cemetery full of limes. It tasted like — I don't know, like a summer evening.

MARNIE: That's a book quote.

ROZ: It is actually in the book. I'm recycling.

[00:08:30]

MARNIE: Let's talk about the car park.

ROZ: [laughs] Okay. So, the multi-storey. A shopping centre asked whether I could put some hives on the roof of their car park, as part of a sustainability thing they were doing. And I said yes, slightly too fast. What I hadn't thought about is that the top floor of a car park in summer is basically a frying pan. Concrete, no shade, heat coming up off the cars. The first July, I went up there and the bees were bearding — that's when they hang out of the front of the hive in a big clump, because it's too hot inside —

JOEL: Like a beard.

ROZ: Like a beard, exactly. And I thought, this isn't fair on them. So we moved them after one season to a shadier spot on a lower level with a green roof, and they were much happier. That was a big lesson. A rooftop is not automatically a good home. You need shade, shelter from wind, and water nearby. If there's no pond or stream within a few hundred metres, you have to provide water, otherwise they'll go and drink from someone's swimming pool or a dripping tap, and then you've got angry neighbours.

MARNIE: Speaking of angry neighbours —

ROZ: Oh, here we go.

MARNIE: — that's one of the biggest worries people have when they think about urban beekeeping. What do you tell people?

ROZ: Talk to them first. Before the bees arrive, not after. Most people are fine once you explain that honeybees aren't interested in them, and that the wasps that bother them at picnics are a completely different animal. I always offer neighbours a jar of honey at the end of the season. It's amazing what a jar of honey does for diplomacy. And — this is important — choose your bees for temperament. Some colonies are just grumpy, and if you've got grumpy bees in a small garden in a city, it's not fair on anyone. You can requeen a grumpy colony with a calmer queen, and in a city that's often the responsible thing to do.

[00:12:15]

JOEL: Let's talk about beginners, because I know you teach a lot of them. What's the biggest mistake new beekeepers make?

ROZ: Honestly? Wanting honey too soon.

MARNIE: Oh, interesting.

ROZ: Everyone gets into bees, at least partly, for the honey. Of course they do, it's magical, you've got a box of insects in your garden and it produces this golden stuff. But in the first year, with a new colony, I tell people: don't take any. Leave it all for the bees.

JOEL: Why?

ROZ: Because the bees didn't make it for you. They made it to get through the winter. A colony in our climate needs something like eighteen to twenty-two kilos of stored honey to make it from October to March, when there's almost nothing flowering and it's too cold to fly most days. They cluster together in a ball and eat their stores, and they shiver their flight muscles to keep the cluster warm, and that burns through a lot of honey. A new colony — say you've started from a nucleus in May, which is how most beginners start — spends its whole first summer just building. It's drawing out wax comb from nothing, which takes an enormous amount of energy. It's raising brood to grow the population. By the end of that first summer, it's often only just got enough put away to survive. If you take some of that, you're taking their winter food, and you'll be feeding them sugar syrup in October and hoping, or you'll open the hive in March and find a dead colony with their heads stuck in empty cells. I've seen that. It's heartbreaking, and it's completely avoidable.

MARNIE: So year one, no jars at all.

ROZ: Year one, no jars. Year two, if the colony's strong and the season's good, you'll probably get a harvest, and it will taste even better because you waited. I actually make my students promise. I make them put their hand on a frame of brood and swear.

JOEL: [laughs] Do you really?

ROZ: No. But I would if I could get away with it.

[00:15:40]

MARNIE: What about the other big one, varroa? For listeners who are new, varroa is a mite — a parasite — that lives on honeybees and spreads viruses, and it's the main reason colonies die in a lot of the world.

ROZ: Yes. Varroa is the thing that keeps me up at night. Every colony in this country has it, or will. It's not a question of whether, it's how many. The mites feed on the developing bees and on adults, and they spread viruses, particularly deformed wing virus, which you can see — the bees come out with crumpled, useless wings. Once the mite numbers get high enough, the colony collapses, usually in autumn or winter.

JOEL: So what do you do?

ROZ: You monitor, and you treat when you need to. Monitoring means counting mites — there are a few ways, I usually do a sugar roll or look at the natural mite drop on a tray under the hive. And then there are various treatments, some based on natural acids, some not, and you have to follow the instructions and the rules carefully, especially if you're taking honey for people to eat. I won't go into specific products, because what's appropriate depends on your country, the time of year and what's licensed where you are, and I'd rather people learned that properly from their local association than from a podcast.

MARNIE: Fair.

ROZ: The main thing I tell beginners is: don't ignore it because your bees look fine. By the time a colony looks unwell from varroa, it's often too late to save it.

[00:18:20]

JOEL: Let's do swarming, because you mentioned Desmond's swarm.

ROZ: “Don't let them swarm.” Desmond's last words to me, basically.

JOEL: So what is swarming, and why do people worry about it in a city?

ROZ: Swarming is how honeybee colonies reproduce. When a colony gets big and crowded in late spring, the bees raise new queens, and then the old queen leaves with roughly half the workers to find a new home. It's completely natural and, honestly, one of the most beautiful things you'll ever see — ten or twenty thousand bees pouring out of the hive and spiralling up into the air. But in a city, a swarm landing on a bus stop or a pram or a café table causes panic. People ring the police. I once collected a swarm from the wing mirror of a parked ambulance.

MARNIE: No.

ROZ: Yes! The paramedics were brilliant about it, they just went and had a cup of tea while I dealt with it.

JOEL: So how do you stop it?

ROZ: You can't stop the urge completely, but you can manage it. Inspect every seven days or so in swarm season — roughly late April to July here — look for queen cells, give them more space before they get crowded, and if they're determined to swarm, do an artificial swarm, which is basically splitting the colony yourself in a controlled way so they think they've swarmed. It's a whole technique; we cover it on the course. The other thing every urban beekeeper should do is sign up to their association's swarm collection list, so if the public find a swarm, they ring someone who knows what they're doing.

[00:21:55]

MARNIE: You're the education officer for the association. What does that actually involve?

ROZ: Oh, everything. I organise the winter lecture programme, I run the mentoring scheme — every new member gets paired with an experienced beekeeper for their first two seasons — I do school visits with an observation hive, which is a glass-sided hive the kids can look into, and I run the beginners' courses.

JOEL: How big is the association now?

ROZ: We're at about a hundred and forty members, which is more than double what it was when I joined. There was a big jump after the first lockdown, actually. Lots of people at home looking at their gardens and thinking, I could do something with that.

MARNIE: Is that a good thing? I feel like there's been a debate about whether there are now too many honeybees in some cities.

ROZ: This is a really important point and I'm glad you raised it. There's evidence from some cities that very high densities of honeybee hives can compete with wild bees — the bumblebees and solitary bees — for flowers. We have something like two hundred and seventy species of bee in this country, and only one of them is the honeybee. The others don't make honey you can harvest, but they're incredibly important pollinators, and many are in decline. So I always say to people: if your main reason for wanting hives is to “save the bees”, the honeybee isn't the one that needs saving. It's a managed animal, like a chicken. If you want to help bees in general, plant flowers, leave a bit of your garden scruffy, don't use pesticides, put up a bee hotel for solitary bees, and push your council to mow verges less often.

JOEL: That's a slightly awkward message from a beekeeper.

ROZ: It is, and some of my colleagues don't love it. But I'd rather people came into beekeeping with their eyes open. Keep honeybees because you're fascinated by them and you'll look after them properly, not because you think a hive is like recycling.

[00:25:30]

[AD BREAK]

MARNIE: Hive Minds is also brought to you by Thornbury Seeds. If you've been listening to Roz and thinking “I should plant more for pollinators”, Thornbury do a pollinator mix that's specifically chosen for small urban gardens and window boxes, with plants that flower from early spring right through to the first frosts. They're peat-free, the packaging is compostable, and the seeds are grown in this country. Head to thornbury-seeds.example.com/hiveminds for a free packet of their wildflower mix with any order. Thanks, Thornbury.

[END AD BREAK]

[00:26:20]

JOEL: Okay, let's talk about stings, because we've got a lot of listener questions about stings.

ROZ: Of course you have.

JOEL: How often do you get stung?

ROZ: Less than people think. Maybe a dozen times a year, mostly when I've been careless — rushing, or doing an inspection on a cold, thundery day when they're cross anyway. A calm colony on a warm afternoon, handled gently, will often let you go through the whole hive without a single sting. What sets them off is fast movement, knocking the frames, crushing bees, strong smells — I don't wear perfume or use scented shampoo on a bee day — and dark, fluffy clothing, because they're programmed to defend against bears and badgers.

MARNIE: Badgers?

ROZ: Badgers will dig out a wasp nest. And honeybees seem to have a strong opinion about anything dark and furry. Which is why bee suits are white.

MARNIE: I learned that the hard way. I wore a black fleece under my suit.

JOEL: Episode fourteen.

MARNIE: Thank you, Joel.

ROZ: The other thing to say is that while most people just get a sore, swollen lump, a small number of people have a serious allergic reaction. If you're thinking of starting, it's worth knowing whether you or anyone in your household is allergic. And beekeepers who've been stung a lot can occasionally develop an allergy over time, so you can't be complacent. On the course we talk about what a serious reaction looks like and when to call for help.

[00:29:45]

MARNIE: Let's do listener questions. We put a call out on social media and got, I think, over two hundred.

JOEL: Two hundred and twelve.

MARNIE: He counted.

JOEL: I counted. First one is from Priyanka, who says: “I live in a flat with a small balcony on the fourth floor. Can I keep bees on it?”

ROZ: Probably not, and I say that gently. A balcony is usually too small to work a hive safely — you need space to stand behind it, put frames down, and get away if things go wrong. The bees' flight path would be right next to your neighbours' windows. And most leases and tenancy agreements don't allow it, and your building insurance almost certainly won't. What I'd suggest instead is getting in touch with your local association about becoming a “bee buddy” — helping an experienced beekeeper with their hives — or asking about community apiaries. And plant your balcony for pollinators. That's a real contribution.

JOEL: Next one is from Tomás: “What's the most surprising thing you've learned about bees?”

ROZ: Oh, that's lovely. Probably the waggle dance. When a forager finds a good patch of flowers, she comes back and does a dance on the comb — a figure-of-eight with a waggling run in the middle — and the angle of the waggle run relative to straight up tells the other bees the direction of the flowers relative to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells them the distance. They're doing trigonometry in the dark, on a vertical surface, while other bees are crawling over them. I've watched it hundreds of times in the observation hive and it still makes the hair on my arms stand up.

MARNIE: Me too, and I've only seen it on video.

JOEL: This one's a bit spicy. From Gwen: “Isn't taking honey from bees exploitative?”

ROZ: It's a fair question and I don't want to dodge it. I think it can be done well or badly, like keeping any animal. Done badly, you take everything, feed them cheap sugar, and treat the colony as a honey machine. Done well, you take only the surplus — what the colony doesn't need — you leave them plenty for winter, you look after their health, and you let them behave like bees. I take much less honey than a commercial beekeeper would, and I'm comfortable with that. But I respect people who'd rather not eat honey at all. There are plenty of ways to be involved with bees without harvesting anything.

JOEL: Last listener question, from Arjun: “How much does it cost to get started?”

ROZ: More than people expect, less than a hobby like sailing. You need a hive, a suit, gloves, a smoker, a hive tool, and some bees. Then there's the course, association membership and insurance, and varroa monitoring. I don't like quoting exact figures on a podcast because prices change and it depends a lot on whether you buy new or second-hand, but the association has a starter list on its website with the current costs, and second-hand equipment can be fine as long as it's properly cleaned, because some bee diseases can survive in old woodwork.

[00:36:10]

MARNIE: I want to ask about the hospital garden, because that's in the book and it made me cry on a train.

ROZ: [pause] Yeah. So, about five years ago, a hospice — it's attached to one of the big hospitals here — asked if I'd put a hive in their garden. One of their nurses had read something about bees and wellbeing and thought patients might like it. I was nervous, honestly. Lots of people who are very ill, families, staff — the last thing anyone needs is a sting or a swarm. So we planned it really carefully. We put the hive behind a hedge, so the bees fly up and over and don't cross the paths. We chose the calmest colony I had. And we built a little viewing window into the fence, at wheelchair height.

JOEL: How did people react?

ROZ: It changed the garden. Patients who hadn't left their rooms for days would ask to be wheeled out to see the bees. People would sit and watch the foragers coming in with their legs packed with pollen — orange, yellow, sometimes this incredible bright blue from a particular flower — and they'd ask me questions. One man, he'd been a carpenter, asked if he could help make a new roof for the hive. He made it in the hospice workshop over a few weeks. He died before it was finished, and his grandson finished it. It's still on the hive.

MARNIE: [quietly] That's the bit.

ROZ: Yeah. That's the bit. Every year we do a small batch of honey from that hive, and it goes to the patients and families. Little jars with handwritten labels. The staff call it “garden gold”.

[00:38:10]

JOEL: Can we do a quick tour of the beekeeping year? Because I think people imagine it's all summer and honey.

ROZ: Oh, it's a whole year. Let me try to do it fast. In January and February, there's almost nothing to do with the bees themselves. They're clustered, you leave them alone, and you just “heft” the hive now and then — you lift the back an inch to feel how heavy it is, so you know whether they've got enough food left. That's when I mend frames, clean equipment, and give talks to anyone who'll listen.

MARNIE: So, us.

ROZ: So, you. March, the first warm days, you see them bringing in pollen from crocuses and willow, and that's the best sign in the world, because pollen means the queen is laying and they're raising brood. April, you do your first proper inspection on a warm, still day, and from then until July you're in swarm season, inspecting every week. May and June are the busiest months of the year for me. In a city, there's sometimes a gap in late June — we call it the June gap — when the spring flowers are finished and the summer ones haven't started, and colonies can actually run short of food just when they're at their biggest. Then the limes flower in July and it's a free-for-all. August is harvest, then varroa treatment, then you make sure they've got their winter stores. September and October, ivy, and you're putting mouse guards on the entrances so mice don't move in for the winter. November and December, rest.

JOEL: Mouse guards.

ROZ: A mouse in a hive in winter is a disaster. They eat the comb, they make a nest, the smell drives the bees mad. A strip of metal with small holes across the entrance stops them, and the bees can still get in and out.

MARNIE: And what about the honey itself — extracting? What does that look like in a city, when you haven't got a farmhouse kitchen?

ROZ: It's sticky. Very, very sticky. I extract in my own kitchen, which is not big. You take the frames of capped honey off the hive, you slice the wax cappings off with a warm knife, you put the frames in an extractor — which is basically a drum that spins them, so the honey flies out by centrifugal force — and then you strain it and let it settle in a bucket with a tap at the bottom. Then you jar it. Every surface in the kitchen ends up sticky for a week, and somehow there's always honey on the light switch. The association has a shared extractor that members can borrow, which is a lifesaver because a decent one isn't cheap.

JOEL: Do you enter honey shows?

ROZ: I did once. There's a whole world of honey shows, with judges who hold your jar up to the light looking for a single speck of wax or a bubble. I got “highly commended” for my cemetery lime honey and was ridiculously proud of it. Then I realised the judge had marked me down because my lid had a tiny scratch, and I decided I didn't have the temperament for competitive honey.

[00:40:30]

JOEL: I want to give people some practical stuff before we wrap up. Say I've listened to this and I'm thinking, maybe next year. What should I do first?

ROZ: Three things. One, find your local beekeeping association and go to a meeting. Most of them have winter talks that anyone can come to. Two, do a proper beginners' course over the winter and spring, so you learn the theory before you're standing in front of an open hive with forty thousand bees looking at you. Three, get some hands-on time with an experienced beekeeper before you get your own bees. Ideally help someone for a full season. Then, if you still want to do it, get your own bees the following spring, start with one colony — or two, ideally, so you can compare them and borrow resources from one to help the other — and get a mentor.

MARNIE: Don't buy bees first.

ROZ: Please don't buy bees first. You'd be amazed how many people order a nucleus online in February, and then ring the association in a panic in May when a box of bees turns up on their doorstep.

[00:42:50]

MARNIE: Before we go, we always end with the quick-fire round. Ready?

ROZ: Oh no. Okay.

MARNIE: Favourite flower for bees.

ROZ: Ivy. Underrated, flowers in autumn when there's nothing else.

JOEL: Favourite honey you've ever tasted.

ROZ: The cemetery lime honey. I said that already, didn't I.

MARNIE: Worst place you've ever collected a swarm.

ROZ: Inside a post box. The postman was not happy.

JOEL: Smoker fuel of choice.

ROZ: Dried pine needles and a bit of hessian. Smells like Christmas.

MARNIE: One thing you wish everyone knew about bees.

ROZ: That the honeybee is one bee out of hundreds of species, and the wild ones need our help more.

[00:45:15]

JOEL: Roz, this has been brilliant. Where can people find you, and the book, and the courses?

ROZ: The book is The Rooftop Hive, it's out in paperback now from Linnet Press, and any bookshop can order it. Please buy it from an independent bookshop if you can. I'm not on social media much, but the association website has all my courses and talks.

MARNIE: And you're running another beginners' course soon, right? I saw a poster.

ROZ: Yes — the next beginners' course starts on Saturday the 14th of March, at the Wharfside Community Centre. It's five Saturday mornings, from ten till one, finishing with a session at the association apiary where everyone gets to open a hive in a suit, with a mentor beside them. It's capped at sixteen people so everyone gets proper time at the hive, and it usually fills up, so book early through the association website. And there are a few bursary places for people who couldn't otherwise afford it — just ask, no explanation needed.

JOEL: Saturday the fourteenth of March at Wharfside, everybody.

MARNIE: Thank you so much, Roz.

ROZ: Thank you both. This was a joy. And Marnie, white fleece next time.

MARNIE: I'm never living that down.

[00:46:40]

[Ukulele jingle]

JOEL: That's it for this episode of Hive Minds. If you enjoyed it, please rate and review us wherever you get your podcasts — it genuinely helps new listeners find the show.

MARNIE: Hive Minds is produced by Ellis Fairweather, with editing by Kiran Toft and our theme music by the Allotment Strummers. Our transcripts are made with the help of automatic transcription software and checked by volunteers, so if you spot a mistake, let us know.

JOEL: Next week: we're talking honey fraud. Is the honey in your supermarket really honey? Spoiler: not always.

MARNIE: Until then, keep your smoker lit —

JOEL: — and your fleece white.

MARNIE: Bye!

[00:47:30] [End of episode. The remaining runtime is a bonus clip: bees in the observation hive, recorded at the hospice garden, with no talking.]

------------------------------------------------------------
